subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Acting
Prime Minister. In view of the serious situation developing between the United States and North Korea will the government make a full statement on that matter, preferably on Monday so that parliament and the people of Canada will know the facts and, in particular, what Canada's position is and will be?

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for the helpful way in which he has phrased his question. The Security Council will be called into urgent session this afternoon at the initiative of the ambassador of the United States to the United Nations. I think that this is a situation where prudence and cool heads will be required.
The Security Council has an obligation in matters that threaten the peace or where there is a violation of the peace. The fact that one of the major powers in the world, the United States, should seek the assistance of the United Nations in overcoming this difficult problem by diplomacy is something I am sure to be welcomed by the Security Council as well as by all of us. Our ambassador has been instructed to use his influence and his presence on the council to see that diplomatic methods are resorted to in trying to meet this difficult and tense situation.
It might be useful for the Security Council to consider a parallel situation when the former secretary general, Dag Hammarskjold, suggested that someone representing him might be sent to China to deal with the situation and to avoid the use of any but peaceful means. It may be that in this situation the Security Council will want to give consideration to the dispatch of someone representing the Secretary General.
I assure my hon. friend that the Canadian government is following the matter very closely. I hope to be seeing the United States ambassador right after orders of the day. I assure my hon. friend and the house that the government is fully conscious of the situation and is following it very carefully.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, while I know the house welcomes the fact that it is being given information, the request from our house leader was that the minister might make a full
January 26, 1968

Inquiries of the Ministry statement on Monday, of course on motions. The minister has complied with the request now, but we are on the orders of the day.
The matter is sufficiently serious, and the interest and responsibility of members is sufficiently grave that, in view of the course followed by the minister, I should like to suggest that we might now revert to motions. He could complete his statement on motions and then there could be comments from representatives of the other parties in the house.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate what my hon. friend has said. I do not have anything further to add at this time. After the meeting of the Security Council today it might be that we could revert to motions; if not, I would follow the suggestion that I make a more complete statement on Monday.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. In view of the fact that the Security Council is meeting today I think it is incumbent upon the government to give us some information at this time concerning what position the Canadian representatives at the United Nations will be taking in respect of the Pueblo incident. I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether Canada will be taking the position that this seizure of a United States ship by the North Korean naval forces constitutes an isolated alleged violation of the freedom of the seas or whether the Canadian government takes the position that this action is a violation of the Korean armistice agreement signed in 1953 and therefore constitutes, in the terms of that agreement, a renewal of the armed attack and challenges the principles of the United Nations. It would seem to be important that Canada's position in this regard be made clear at once.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend will agree that this is a situation in respect of which we ought to be careful about the judgments we make. There is the position put forward by the United States, as I said the day before yesterday, that the ship was not plying in the territorial seas of North Korea. This is a matter of fact which undoubtedly will be discussed in the United Nations Security Council. There have been some allegations of violations on the other side. I do not wish to prejudge these. Until there has been the fullest examination I think it would be wise to suspend judgment.
[Mr. Fulton.)

It is this kind of situation I had in mind when I observed that it might be desirable at some point for a representative of the Secretary General himself to go to the area. Then we would have to see what developments follow.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I was not asking the minister to make a judgment concerning whether or not there had been a violation of freedom of the seas. I was asking whether or not the Canadian government considers this to be a separate act in dispute between the United States government and North Korea, or whether he considers it to be a violation of the Korean armistice of 1953 and therefore that Canada would have a responsibility to deal with any violation of that agreement.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said the other day this seems to be a matter which does not involve the United Nations directly, or Canada as a component of the United Nations force. The ship in question was not, I believe, under the command of the United Nations in Korea. However, this will be a question that the other side will dispute and it is a matter which will have to be examined. I did refer to the allegation of certain other violations. These too may come within the purport of the agreement, not the agreement of 1957 but that of July 27, 1953.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a supplementary question, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he is casting a doubt on the statement of the United States government that the ship was in international and not in North Korean waters.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: I do not think I have said anything that would in any way cast doubt on the position taken by the United States.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: I understood the minister to say there was an allegation by the United States. Is there not anything more positive than that?

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext:
I said there was an allegation that the Pueblo was plying in the territorial sea off North Korea. I did not say we agreed with that, but I said that was the allegation made. This undoubtedly will be one of the facts to be examined by the Security Council. I want to clearly indicate, and I am sure my hon. friend in this matter, so
January 26, 1968
important as it is to the peace, will not want to add to the difficulty, that we have not in any way indicated that the position taken by the United States is not one that can be substantiated.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. Every time a question is asked here that disturbs the minister for external affairs he suggests the person asking the question is not in favour of peace. I reject that allegation.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: This is not the first time I have heard this from the minister. I will stand with anybody on my record here in respect of maintaining peace in the world. We are entitled to ask questions and entitled to get clear statements from the minister. He has suggested to us that there is some doubt as to whether the statement of the United States government is clear.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Then he attempts to accuse me of falsifying the issue.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: I have a further supplementary question.

subtopic: NORTH KOREA-REFERENCE TO SECURITY COUNCIL-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister, in view of the complex issues and the fact that perhaps international laws are involved in an incident of this sort, whether our representative at the Security Council will suggest that, in addition perhaps to other interim actions, the complex issues be referred either to the world court or some other international tribunal which could take a judicial approach to this matter?

I was not making any suggestion about his concern; I was simply trying as carefully as I could in the face of this situation not to complicate a matter that now will be considered by the Security Council, in the hope
Inquiries of the Ministry that a pacific means will be used to resolve a problem that is of great danger.

Perhaps I might answer a question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir). He asked, first, whether the department intends to remove the pilotage station from North Sydney-in other words to change the base. At present the eight pilots are divided into two four-man watches who man the station 24 hours a day, week on and week off. There is living accommodation for them on the station and the pilot boat is based there. Their dispatch instructions come from the pilotage office in Sydney.
Modern methods of communication make it possible for ships to advise the pilotage office of their expected time of arrival well in advance of the time when a pilot is needed and, consequently, it is no longer necessary to maintain a visual lookout at pilot stations. We have therefore closed many of the stations that previously provided living accommodation, and pilots are now dispatched directly from their homes. This system is to be implemented in Sydney within the next few months. The base of operation for the pilot boat will continue to be North Sydney, and pilots will be transported to and from their assignments on the boat operating from its present location.
The hon. member has also asked whether the department intends to remove the services of pilots from Sydney harbour. The department recognizes the continuing need for a pilotage service in Sydney harbour and: there is no intention of doing away with this service.

speechtext:

On clause 2-Broadcasting policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it would be helpful, but I point out that the committee might consider the fact that we are now on the thirteenth day of our deliberations of this bill. If one adds the 12 days which the parliamentary committee on films, broadcasting and assistance to the arts took to consider the bill clause by clause, the total comes to 25 days, and as one who is deeply interested in and concerned about the efficient management of parliamentary business I feel we all have an obligation to exercise a bit of restraint and self-discipline. This is no criticism of the speeches which have been made; it relates, rather, to the way in which the debate has been developing.
I was interested to note that in the United Kingdom parliament, many of whose rules we have adopted in our own system, they were able last week to dissolve the last remnants of the British empire in the course of a debate which lasted two days and during which speeches were made by the principal people in the house including the prime minister, the chancellor of the exchequer, the leader of the opposition and the leader of the
January 26, 1968

Liberal party. In that time the British house considered the far reaching policy implications of the government decision and had a vote on the issue.
I am not suggesting for one minute, of course, that a bill as important as this one in connection with broadcasting could be given such brief treatment but I do feel, and I mean this very sincerely, that if we expect to be at all credible as an instrument for the consideration of legislation-and I think we would all subscribe to this wish-we should exercise a bit of self-restraint. Really, 13 days consideration of this bill after 12 days consideration by the parliamentary committee should lead one to anticipate more rapid progress.
Hear, hear.

As a member of this house I rise to say that I do not need a lecture from anybody. I am not happy about what the committee is doing and I do not think I need a lecture on how the business of the house should be carried on. I was elected by my constituents to do my duty as I see it and to speak on the activities of the C.B.C. whenever necessary. I feel I am bound to do this, and I do not appreciate lectures from anybody about what I should, or should not do.

I would not want the committee to vote on this clause and on the amendment I moved without hearing some comment from the minister. May I summarize the arguments I presented in favour of the amendment last night? The bill provides that the publicly owned network is required to contribute to the development of national unity. I said that although I had some misgivings about the inclusion of these words at all, if they are important they ought surely to be a charge to all broadcasters both public and private. I would point out that private television and radio stations do have the right to editorialize, and I suggest that if such stations come into the hands of people who do not believe in national unity or the maintenance of Canadian confederation they could freely run all the editorials they wished denouncing confederation.
I also mentioned that there are more private radio and television stations in Canada than there are public ones and that if this aspect is important at all it should be incumbent on these people, too, to contribute to the development of national unity. If the minister does not believe that this is important, I should like to know why.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this same
subject, I wonder whether the hon. member's argument cannot be turned so as to mean exactly the opposite. Like him, I have some doubts as to the advisability of including that paragraph in the bill, because its contents seems to me such a matter of course. I also share certain doubts as to the scope of the paragraph and the interpretations that can be made of it.
It is so normal to provide that a public broadcasting system will contribute to Canadian solidarity that the mere fact of mentioning it, of writing it out in full, may lead some people to believe that it is not a matter of promotion but of propaganda, which is, as I can testify, far from the intentions, both of the government, that has drafted the legislation, and of the committee which has considered the matter.
Personally, I would be most favourable to the deletion of this paragraph. It seems superfluous. It seems to me that, by including it, we are giving to certain people cause to think that there is a suggestion of propaganda, which is incorrect.
On the other hand, I would oppose still more the extension of the scope of this paragraph to all stations. I think that if this paragraph is justified somewhere, which I doubt, this justification is stronger where a public body financed with public moneys is involved.
So, I am against the amendment precisely because I question the advisability of the paragraph. The only justification I can find for it-and this is hardly worth saying-is that a Canadian institution cannot be used against the interests of Canada. Since this would be redundant, I believe that it should not be extended any further. Nothing would be gained, save bringing about still more erroneous interpretations.
Therefore, I think we should leave this paragraph where it is, emphasize it as little as possible and consider it as something that is said, even though it is needless to say it. Otherwise, it would be contrary to the true spirit of the wording and would create still more doubt and suspicion as to propaganda. I cannot understand that the hon. member who questions the present paragraph would now extend its scope.

I know the hon. member for Hochelaga shares the doubt which some of us have about whether this wording should be in the bill at all. He said so. I am sure the
January 26, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting minister herself was concerned about the abuse which could follow the presence of such wording. However, I would urge the hon. member for Hochelaga and the minister to reconsider their position respecting the amendment, and I do so on two grounds.
[DOT] (12 noon)
If I followed the hon. member for Hochelaga correctly, and I know I did, in effect what he was saying was, "I am doubtful whether it is wise at all to have these words, and if it is unwise let us limit the unwisdom to the public sector only and not spread it further."
That is what he said.

Yes, that is what he said, and to me it does not appear to be very logical. If it is there at all you do not make it wise by limiting it to the C.B.C.; but if there is value in having it, then there is value in imposing the same moral obligation, which is what these words constitute, on the private sector.
There is another important reason why the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, ought to be considered favourably by members opposite who, I am sure, are as concerned about this problem as those of us who are speaking on it from this side. This is the fact that there is specific wording in subclause (d) to the effect that the broadcasting system as a whole should provide reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy.
I suggest that is an important qualification in that subclause, in order that some management persons in the C.B.C., or in a private station cannot exclude people who may differ with them on the ground that in their opinion something may be said that is against Canadian unity. The clause is badly worded the way it is now.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Hochelaga, whom I have known and admired for many years, where is the moral superiority and logic in saying that anyone who wants to destroy Canada can do so if he has enough money? If he has enough money he can buy up all the prime time on television and radio stations across Canada and carry on his propaganda to destroy the country. That is the implication of this.
In a way we are in the position where we cannot talk against motherhood. If we say take away these words, it may be contended that we are against Canadian unity. If this

moral obligation is to be placed in the law, surely it should be applicable to the entire broadcasting system. There is no reason, on this point, that there should be a difference between public and private broadcasting.
On reading the reports of the broadcasting committee discussions I noticed that the objection to placing this subclause higher up in clause 2 came from some people with private broadcasting experience. They do not want to be burdened with this. They are ready to burden the management of the C.B.C. with this provision, but not the management of private broadcasting companies.
I would like to hear better logic than I heard from the hon. member for Hochelaga to justify that kind of result but, as I say, in addition to that there is the fact that if we accepted the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond it would place the contribution to Canadian unity in the context which specifically permits reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy. The manner of contributing to Canadian unity and building Canadian unity obviously differs in the minds of various people across this country.
There are all sorts of ideas in people's minds as to what in fact contributes to Canadian unity and what in fact does not, and how a stronger Canadian unity can be built in the future. Obviously that kind of public controversy should be permitted. I am certain I do not have to persuade the minister and the hon. member for Hochelaga on that point.
I suggest it is much better to have the reference to this in the clause which specifically recognizes the value and the need for reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy. I do not intend to speak at length because we have spent a long time already on this bill. I have not spoken previously in the committee stage, but I do so now to urge the minister and hon. members opposite to accept an amendment which is reasonable, sensible, and which will carry forward their intention throughout the entire broadcasting system.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the stand taken today by the New Democratic party. I am an independentist. Some will say that I am acting against national unity, that at present, independentists have the right to buy time on private television stations and that the C.B.C. offers us free
January 26, 1968

time on the program pertaining to provincial affairs, but if we are deprived of the democratic means of making our views known, where shall we turn?
Mr. Chairman, I am against the use of violence or bombs to spread ideas, because I believe in democratic methods. Now, the principal democratic method is freedom of speech, and now some want to deprive us of our right to freedom of expression on television.
What means could we then resort to if we are prevented from using the democratic means? Do we prefer that violence be substituted to the freedom of speech? Such approach is completely unthinkable on the part of the New Democratic party.
It is the democratic party.

It is the democratic party.
Once adopted in the field of television and broadcasting, we have no assurance that similar legislation will not be passed for newspapers? There you are, democracy is deprived of its true meaning.
Those who like so often to observe what happens in the British parliament in London, their homeland, have probably noticed that independentist or separatist members from Wales and Scotland have the right to sit in that house and that they benefit from the freedom of speech granted to all through mass media. They are allowed to exercise their right of speech. But, today, the ground is being prepared to interfere for the first time with freedom of speech.
Let us take a specific example. In 1942, the Canadian government organized a plebiscite asking the Canadian people whether or not it was in favour of conscription. Now, if the government had said: We are having conscription and those who are against it are against national unity, could we say that Quebec, were 95 per cent of the people voted against conscription, would have been denied the right to express its view over the Canadian radio and television networks because that would have been contrary to Canadian unity and because someone had decreed that it was contrary to Canadian unity?
Mr. Chairman, I ask the members of the New Democratic party to think about that. A while ago, I heard the hon. member for Hoch-elaga (Mr. Pelletier) go over the ideas expressed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie).
In his amendment, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond mentions Canadian unity.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting The hon. member for Hochelaga did not use the same expression. He said: Canadian solidarity. That is the term he used, and I was struck by it.
I am ready to acknowledge my solidarity with the whole Canadian people, from the Atlantic to the shores of the Pacific. But Canadian unity means to be one, to be part of the same group. What is meant by this oneness? Is it oneness of spirit? Does it include unity of religion? Does it include unity of political views? What does it mean?
The hon. member for Hochelaga speaks of solidarity and I am ready to make common cause with everybody.
I think that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, as well as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), were referring to subclause (g) (iv) where we can read:
contribute to the development of national unity-
To that I would agree.
The New Democratic party has included in its platform the theory of two nations. The Conservative party as well as the Liberal party, through its leader the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), have accepted the theory of two nations: the French-Canadian nation and the English-Canadian nation. Unity within each nation. Canadian unity comes from the unity between each nation. Canadian unity comes from the unity between two nations; it is then an international unity. That is not the same thing.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Then a term has been used here and I wonder if the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond really thought about it when drafting his amendment. But I think that it is badly drafted and that he did not realize all the implications of his amendment.
I heard a while ago the hon. member for York South state that Canadian television should not be prejudicial to Canadian interests. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am firmly and sincerely convinced that when I am advocating unity in Quebec, I am not prejudicial to the interests of Canada. On the contrary, I think that it is in the best interests of Canada that Quebec should be independent. But who is going to decide that? Is it the C.B.C.? Is it the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh)?
Mr. Chairman, one can realize that such an amendment is senseless. I agree that subclause (gXiv) could be deleted, because I feel that it does not mean much.

When one refers to national unity, the meaning to me is French-Canadian unity, but there is an English-Canadian unity too. This is the general principle already accepted by
N.D.P., Liberal and Conservative members, in fact by all the members in the house: there are two nations in Canada. Since there are two nations in Canada, we must therefore speak of international unity or unity between the two nations. Nobody can deny that.
Though the subclause is somewhat meaningless, I believe it would be better to take it out altogether, as we cannot leave with the C.B.C. or the hon. Secretary of State the decision of saying what is for the sake of national unity or against it. It would be too large a responsibility for the C.B.C.
I am categorically and squarely opposed to the amendment of the New Democratic party for the reasons I have mentioned and I will say this: If you try to deprive the independ-entists of the democratic means they have, you will force them to resort to other methods.
Today, you can at least say that we are promoting our ideas in a democratic calm and peaceful way without resorting to violence or other similar means. Why? Because we realize that democratic means are more practical and more normal in this 20th century; but if you try to deprive us of those means, you will be the first responsible within this parliament if the independentists resort to more violent means. Why seek this? Think of your amendment, gentlemen, and you will be the first to vote against it. Of that I am sure.

Mr. Chairman, in commenting on the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond I should like to say that I support it wholeheartedly on the ground that if it is good for the publicly owned sector of the television and radio world of Canada to be promoting national unity, it should also be good to have the privately owned sector of the television and radio world supporting the same idea. I agree 100 per cent with the hon. member for York South when he points out that one cannot move to delete the phrase, "contribute to the development of national unity", which appears in paragraph (g) of clause 2, without being accused of hatred and wanting to tear the nation apart which is something like opposing motherhood, although I know that many members of the N.D.P. do oppose motherhood by their favouritism toward abortion. No one would think of

bringing in an amendment to remove this phrase from paragraph (g) (iv).
It would be interesting to many members of the house, I am certain, to ascertain or learn whether the hon. member for Hoch-elaga, since he does not believe that this part of paragraph (g) should be extended to paragraph (d), is thinking of moving that subparagraph (iv) of paragraph (g) be removed. I do believe that the private sector and the public sector should be on the same footing. I believe the hon. member for York South when speaking expressed wonder concerning why this section appeared only in the publicly owned sector of the act and not in the privately owned sector. I should like to remind members of the house that it is only the C.B.C., the publicly owned section of the radio and television world in Canada, which put von Thadden on a national network. Do you think that that contributed to national unity in this country? It was only the C.B.C. that had Lincoln Rockwell on a program of their section of the radio and television world.
Perhaps the cabinet has come to the conclusion that it should put a rule in here that would help control the nationally owned section of the television and radio world and is a little fearful of extending that same authority to the privately owned sector. But, bear in mind that the privately owned sector up to date has not caused the offence to those who are strongly in favour of national unity that the C.B.C. has caused in the past. The amendment that the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond has moved is justified completely by the fact that the amendment is based on paragraph (g) (iv). I recognize that the Speaker having to preside over the discussion with complete impartiality, is entitled to ask the assistance of the official translators.
This is quite normal and the Speaker or the chairman of the committees of the whole could not be asked to give an official translation, since they must be fair-minded. It is not up to either of them to make the translation.
That requirement of the legislator that the Speaker read a motion in French and in English is so fair and wise that on reading the English text of this motion, I find two phrases

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting which have been mistranslated. Personally I would hesitate to translate them, because it is difficult to find the proper terms in French to convey their meaning.
For instance, are we going to say "opportunite balancee" for "balanced opportunity" and translate word for word? I know we have "balanced feeds" for livestock, but are we going to say "opportunite balancee"? speechtext:
This paragraph was stood in view of the amendment moved to it by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. He asked me to look at it and see whether I might accept it. I have done that, Mr. Chairman, and have told him why I cannot accept
January 26, 1968	COMMONS
it. I am sure he will want to say something further before other questions are put, and after he has said something I might make a contribution. I recall he did provide copies in both languages.

Mr. Chairman, my amendment to paragraph (c) was to add between the words "expression" and "subject" in line 19 thereof as follows:
-and the right of Canadians to receive all broadcast programs available to them.
So that the amended clause would read as follows:
(c) all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for programs they broadcast but the right to freedom of expression and the right of Canadians to receive all broadcast programs available to them subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations is unquestioned.
My French being what it is I will not bother to read the French version, but it is available.
The reason behind my amendment is a simple one, and I did speak to it the other night. We want to be careful in this bill to preserve freedom of expression along with the duties of broadcasters. I therefore thought it appropriate to add these words. Having the right to freedom of expression, we should also have the right to freedom to receive the programs that are broadcast.
A similar amendment to mine had been moved by another hon. member which added the words "by any means whatsoever", but I thought this carried the concept too far. This would have left it open to the interpretion that there should be no interference in any way with any kind of cable distribution system or any other method of rebroadcasting or distributing programs. My amendment merely reserves the right to receive all programs. I believed that by removing those offensive words, which I thought went too far, my amendment would be acceptable.
The minister has indicated that she is not prepared to accept the amendment, and she has been kind enough to give some of her reasons. However, since there has been so much agitation and a fair amount of lobbying on this question, and so much has been made of the right of an individual who has a T.V. set to watch whatever programs he desires, I feel a refusal to accept this amendment would be the worst kind of censorship. In my opinion, the bill should specifically state that we want to preserve the right to receive all programs, in the same manner and to the same extent
DEBATES	6039
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting that we felt it necessary to include in this clause the right to freedom of expression.
If the minister does not want to accept the amendment, then I hope she will be kind enough to indicate her reasons and whether a variation of the amendment would be acceptable. In other words, Mr. Chairman, would I be fair if I were to ask the minister whether her objection is simply to the ideal of emphasizing the freedom to receive, or is it based on the fact that, as worded, the amendment is capable of an interpretation that would create difficulty for regulatory authorities in the control of cable distribution systems, and so on, and the solution of problems posed thereby? Perhaps the minister would say a few words about that.

Mr. Chairman, the objection I have to this amendment found support both from the Department of Justice and the Board of Broadcast Governors. In a general way, may I say that I do not think any of us believe there is or should be a restriction on the reception of programs that are received in the normal course. However, signals must come from a properly licensed station. For example, if a pirate station were set up outside the 12-mile limit, although the people might be able to receive its broadcasts, we would not want them to receive them unless the station were licensed. Being a pirate station it would not be licensed and the B.B.G. would have no authority over it.
Technically it would be possible to set up a broadcast or a rebroadcast station and make its programs available to everyone. However, I do not think the B.B.G. should be required to license them simply because such stations are technically feasible. Other considerations come into play, such as whether or not a C.A.T.V. or a rebroadcast station of some kind should be licensed in a given area. Sometimes the B.B.G. turns down such applications because they believe that a broadcasting station will at some time in the future be built in the area and this would be more in the interests of the community concerned.
The difficulty that both justice and the B.B.G. inform me they see in this amendment is that the phrase it seeks to add to the bill means different things to different people. They feel that it would make the bill unnecessarily restrictive if it were open to the interpretation that signals that were echnically possible of transmission ought to be received by all. These signals may come from a
January 26, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting C.A.T.V. station, or an originating station within or without the 12-mile limit.
There is no quarrel wih the proposition that operators who are licensed and lawfully transmitting signals should be able to broadcast to all. However, we do get into this problem. Consider, for example, the C.A.T.V. operator. Let us say that he wishes to rebroadcast four United States signals. In giving this operator a licence the B.B.G. requires that he also carry at least the national program of Canada from his local station. If people have the right to receive all programs, this operator technically could pick up 10 or 12 signals, but he would be able to transmit only about six. So a conflict arises there in that the hon. member contends that people have the right to receive whatever programs are available to them, and these programs would be available if the C.A.T.V. operator broadcast them.
The law officers of the crown and our technical advisers, the Board of Broadcast Governors, do not feel there should be any stricture on the right to receive programs, any more than there is a stricture on the right to read newspapers. But if parliament were to endorse such a broad principle and say that all programs should be available to the people, this may cause considerable difficulty in the application of our licensing requirements which have to be set out in the different parts of the act.
Might I ask the hon. lady a question. Does she mean by her remarks that in the eventuality a pirate broadcasting station were to be set up outside the three-mile limit-
It is 12 miles.

-the government is reserving unto itself the right to prohibit people from receiving such signals, be they radio signals or television signals? Does her rejection of the amendment proposed by the hon. member amount to this?

It would appear from what the minister has said that part of the difficulty arises because my amendment includes the phrase "all programs". I am reluctant to drop the point. I understand the minister's dilemma, but I do not think we are too far apart. Suppose I put in the expression "and the right to receive programs" rather than "all programs". That might ease the difficulty.
My reasoning is simple. In this clause we are pointing to responsibilities which the government feels it is necessary to enunciate. I feel there is a right to receive programs, subject to rules and regulations, just as there is a right to freedom of expression, subject to rules and regulations. This seems to be the place at which to include a reference to this right. I gather that the minister herself feels that this is a proper attitude to take and that our difference arises from the wording itself. If I am correct in this assumption I wonder whether the hon. lady would mind indicating whether she thinks it is possible to work out a form of words which would simply remind us of the right to receive programs, and to have those words included in the bill without offending the feelings of those who will be called upon to handle this act and who fear it might be made unworkable.

I am not happy about the proposal to put this in subclause (c), because this subclause deals with the obligations and rights of licencees. It might be better in (e) or in a separate subclause altogether dealing with the right of Canadians to hear programs. I have told the hon. member what my advisers think of this. I am told that the ramifications are too wide, and I am advised not to accept the amendment.
I realize, of course, that nothing sinister is intended by the hon. member-it seems absurd that anything sinister could come from him-but I think, on reflection, that I
January 28, 1968	COMMONS
should accept the advice of my officials in this regard.

Might I ask another question? The minister suggested there might be a possibility of incorporating the amendment in a separate subclause. I had the impression from her words, and their manner of delivery, that she was loath to turn it down and would like to find some way round the difficulties she mentioned. She says she is bothered because we are dealing with a subclause affecting licencees. I have the feeling that deep down she recognizes there is discrimination as between those who receive a loud and clear signal and those further away who get a much poorer signal but who still have the right to listen to it and who, by the use of cablevision, would be able to get a loud and clear signal just as though they were living near the border. Would the minister consider the matter from this point of view? Perhaps she could come up with a proposal of her own along the lines put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, and incorporate it in the bill.

Possibly the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona would like 2 (c) to stand again. This would give him a chance to talk with some of the law officers of the crown in an attempt to find words which could be placed in a separate subclause.

I think that would be a good idea. I am sure it is the wish of the committee generally that we should express approval of the right to receive. Let us leave it until Monday and in the meantime try to find a formula which will not have the consequences that the minister's advisers fear.

I have not intervened in this discussion so far, but I believe it would be a serious error of judgment if we were to leave the subject in the absence of an indication that there is no restriction on the right to receive programs. I understand the minister's position. She has been given certain advice and feels compelled to pay attention to it. But the only inference flowing from what she has said is that there may be, on the part of the government, the right to prohibit reception in some cases. I hope the minister and her officials, bearing this in mind, will strive diligently to come up with something which rejects such an implication.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
Therefore I sincerely hope that you will give your support to the application that has been presented to your department from citizens of the town of Napanee.
Thank you, I remain,
Yours very truly,
Lome A. Smart, Mayor of Napanee.
Franchises have been handed out all around us but Napanee has been ignored. Just an hour ago I communicated by telephone with the town of Picton, which is the county town of the county of Prince Edward. I am pleased to hear that a franchise has been granted by the government for C.A.T.V. there. Picton can well use such a service because most of the town is situated at a low altitude, below and on the north side of MacAulay's mountain. I am glad to hear that a franchise has been granted there to a local and reliable firm.
My question is one being asked by hundreds of Napanee citizens, why is the franchise for Napanee being withheld? I note that there is at least one other application besides that of Mr. Dawson. I note that it is in the name of an Ottawa man, who has made an application to serve the towns of Prescott, Gananoque and my native town of Napanee.
I contend, and I am sure all members of the committee will agree, that these franchises should go to applicants who are local, taxpaying citizens of these towns if they are able to perform the necessary service. The government has no right to grant these franchises to large syndicates which operate remotely out of larger centres, and which have no real local interest in a town like Napanee other than the acquisition of thousands of dollars or revenue per year. This revenue would be siphoned off to the larger centres and would not be spent within the local municipality. For that reason I repeat what I said last June 22.
I contend, and I am sure the minister agrees, that a responsible local application such as this from a resident of the municipality, where cable facilities are economically and physically feasible, should be quite in order. Indeed, it should command top priority. I contend that the Department of Transport has no right to withhold a franchise for this service providing the operator of it agrees to comply fully with the regulations governing the lighting and marking of his tower so that it will not endanger the flight of aircraft.
As Mayor Smart pointed out in his letter, franchises have been granted in other towns

in Ontario, and yet the Napanee franchise is refused for no good reason at all. I appeal to the hon. lady, whose bill we are dealing with, to use her good influence to see that a franchise is granted to the local applicant for the town of Napanee, in order that the best interests of all may be served. Television reception in Napanee is far from perfect because of the town's low altitude. We are entitled to prompt consideration and I intend to ask for early appointments with both the Secretary of State and the Department of Transport for Mayor Smart and his council-

Mr. Chairman, I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend but I have absolutely nothing to do with that licence. It is the happy duty of my hon. friend, the Minister of Transport, to reign over that particular empire. Much as I would like to see Mayor Smart and his people, it would only be wasting their time.

I fully realize that the hon. lady does not have the responsibility, but I have merely asked her to use her influence with the Minister of Transport.
I congratulate the hon. lady for the constructive criticism she made of the C.B.C. not very long ago. Her criticism was of programming and management. Of late, criticism has been levelled by the general public at that body. I just wish to say that I have received many letters of condemnation regarding some of the ill taste that has been displayed in programming. I am sure that the management of the C.B.C., both executive and programming, will respond to the reasonable and firm protests of the Canadian viewing public, and will exercise proper restraint with respect to the character and quality of T.V. programs.
I remind them that the character of these programs to a great extent is commensurately reflected in the character of our people. Their influence on our people is in direct ratio to the quality of the programming. In this regard I am reminded of that ever reliable axiom, "Habit crystallizes into character."
I also wish to say that this chamber is the place where this bill can be turned into good legislation, legislation that will be an influence for good and which will provide reliable guidance to the executives of the C.B.C.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Although I am also one of those who at the present time asks for better value for our dollars invested and for better economic practice in the C.B.C., I am still one of those who
January 26, 1968

has confidence that despite our present troubles good judgment and good management will result from our current far-flung national criticism of this body and from the legislation that we are slowly but efficiently bringing forth.
I have heard that members of the cabinet are becoming very impatient at the time we are spending on this bill. I should like to remind these impatient ministers, whose interests are now diverted to personal glories on the Liberal leadership hustings, that this is a very poor time for them to portray impatience because the majority of people look on this legislation with intense interest. I should like to remind the government that Canada deserves-and let us hope that from our deliberations here, will get-better broadcasting services and better value for the tax dollar.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to congratulate the minister for the flexibility in accepting the amendment moved by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. In so doing, I believe she has shown that she is willing to listen to criticism from the opposition side of the house. I am of the opinion that we could rapidly conclude this aspect of the debate with regard to the content of C.B.C. programming, matters of good taste, additional forms of programming and so on, if the minister would simply rise and say to the house, "I will recommend to the C.B.C. that in its operation it pay due respect to the principles enunciated by the Minister of Justice when he made a statement to the nation that in his opinion the state has no right to enter the bedrooms of the nation". From then on I am sure we would be quite safe. Would the minister do that?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member should know that it is not under the 1958 statute, and is not likely to be under the current statute, my responsibility to give instructions to the C.B.C. So far as the Minister of Justice's principles are concerned, I think he can stand on his own feet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There has been a suggestion that subclause 2 (c) stand. Is it the wish of the committee that this be done now?

Mr. Chairman, I would prefer to speak to the question of subclause 2 (c) today rather than on Monday. However, I will be here on Monday as well as today. I regret having to indulge in personalities, but I must say, after listening to the hon. Secretary of
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting State when she appeared before the broadcasting committee-I have the minutes of proceedings and evidence here in front of me and will read them to you shortly-and from her explanation today that it is quite apparent she does not understand a community antenna television operation. There is nothing the matter with the C.A.T.V. operation either in Canada or elsewhere in the world. The comments which have been directed toward the C.A.T.V. operation are beyond my belief for ignorance.
I was first elected to this House of Commons in 1962 and saw the hon. member for Niagara Falls here when I came in as a member of the opposition. There is no member of this house for whom I have a higher regard. She stood up today and said that she has a recommendation from the Department of Justice. I marked down her words. She said: "I am bound to accept this recommendation of the Department of Justice and the Board of Broadcast Governors". I should like to ask her why she and I stood up together and voted the Diefenbaker government out of office when we would not accept a ruling of the Department of Justice from a man by the name of Dreidger who was advising the Diefenbaker government regarding import and export taxes. It is a very short time since she and I stood together and refused to accept the statement of the Department of Justice as passed on to us by the then minister of justice, Hon. Donald Fleming.
In 1963 the hon. member for Niagara Falls and I stood together with many other members of this house and turned out the Diefenbaker administration. Now, after we have come to the seats of the treasury benches we get another opinion from the Department of Justice. If the Department of Justice makes such magnificent recommendations that they must be accepted by the minister and if they are so important she is bound to stand by them, why has Mr. Dreidger been moved to Hamburg, Germany where he is the third or fourth assistant consul.
1 he Chairman: Order, please. I am sure the hon. member realizes that he is now well outside the ambit of the clause which is before us. Perhaps he would return to the actual subclause.

I am referring to the statement of the Secretary of State to the effect that she is bound to accept the recommendation of the Department of Justice. I am pointing out that in the past she did not consider herself bound
January 26, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting to accept the recommendation of the Department of Justice. I have made the point that if Mr. Dreidger is so wonderful, why is he still not in the Department of Justice.
Just now the Secretary of State made the statement that if the people have the right to receive all the programs on the air what do we do about places where there are 12 programs available on the air but the receiving set of the C.A.T.V. can only bring in seven? This would mean that there were five which could not be received. All Canadians have the right to read whatever magazines and periodicals they wish to read. Thank God the cabinet has not started to interfere in that field. Does that mean we must buy every magazine and periodical? We have the right to buy them, but when we do not buy them this does not interfere with the importance of the right to information wherever we can get it. If we subscribe to a service which brings in only five out of the eight or ten available channels on the air, that is our business; it is our money we are spending.
As I said before in the month of October, I believe, when this bill was first introduced, this is perfect legislation for the past but pays no attention to the future development of radio and television in this world. I sincerely believe that television as we know it today is on the way out and that the C.A.T.V. systems will take over the entire field in time. On the question of C.A.T.V., I have in my hand here minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 6 of the standing committee on broadcasting, films and the assistance to the arts for Tuesday, November 28. On that day Hon. Judy La-Marsh, Secretary of State, was present. As reported at page 166, in answering a question asked by Mr. Jamieson, Miss LaMarsh said this:
-I am not very familiar with the economics of them-
That is, the C.A.T.V. systems. Then on page 167, in answer to another question by Mr. Jamieson, Miss LaMarsh said:
-but of my own knowledge I do not know that much detail about it.
Then, as reported at page 167 in answer to a question of mine she said:
And they fill those five channels with other than local stations. The local station is not capable of being received on the C.A.T.V. that one gets in one's individual home. It blanks out.
Now, in respect of that third quotation I have given you I say to the Chairman and to others in the House of Commons that every time a C.A.T.V. operation has been licensed

in the Dominion of Canada the application has been submitted through the Department of Transport which refers it to the Board of Broadcast Governors. Finally, the licence is granted if the department so decides. There has never been a C.A.T.V. licence granted in Canada which did not have, as the first specification, that the system must pick up the local available Canadian station. Someone will say that he knows of a C.A.T.V. system on which one cannot receive a local station.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
If there is a C.A.T.V. station in this country on which you do not get a Canadian station, and I know for a fact there are several, it is because no Canadian station is available in that territory. I am told by men who know, one of whom is generally sitting in the house, that there are C.A.T.V. installations in British Columbia that have nothing but United States stations on them because no Canadian stations can be received. If a Canadian station could be received the Department of Transport, under the Minister of Transport, would specify in the licence that the Canadian station had to be on the dial of the C.A.T.V. installation. There is not a single C.A.T.V. installation in Canada on which a Canadian channel that is available has been shut off, because the Department of Transport has always specified that Canadian stations which are available in the location must be carried on C.A.T.V.
If the Secretary of State is going to worry about the fact that some wires today in the cable system will only bring you five or seven channels when there may be ten or 12 channels available in the area, let her stop worrying too much about that. The C.A.T.V. systems operation is progressing so fast, and I have mentioned this in the house before but take the time to repeat it today, that wires which will take up to 30 channels are now available. If the Secretary of State, the Department of Transport and the Board of Broadcast Governors are going to worry about some places having 12 programs available but only five channels on the C.A.T.V. installation, let me assure them that a wire can be put in which will carry more channels on the C.A.T.V. installation in Canada than there are programs available for the area. This is a straight statement of fact which nobody can deny. In Hendersonville, North Carolina, there is a C.A.T.V. installation today that has 23 channels on the wire although there are not 23 programs available in that area of North Carolina to fill these
January 26, 1968

channels. They have a wire there that is bringing in all the available channels, with a lot of other blank channels as well. I mention 23 channels to you because to my knowledge that is the maximum in use at the present time.
Let me remind the minister that the electrical industry in the world today can produce wires that will carry 30 channels, so she need not worry about any channel being kept off by the C.A.T.V. system. If a channel were kept off the C.A.T.V. operator would be doing so contrary to the requirements of the Department of Transport.
This is not the principal point in this discussion on the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. This point involves the right to receive programs available in an area. I have said in this house many times, and I repeat it again now-the little episode which occurred at noon today does not bother me in the slightest-that I have the highest regard for the hon. member for Niagara Falls. I am not buttering her up but stating an opinion I have held for several years. One of the things I admire about her is that she is not only the Secretary of State, she is also the hon. member for Niagara Falls.
When there was a move afoot, on behalf of certain interests I will not name, to move the Barrie T.V. station into the metropolitan Toronto area where it would interfere with the reception of two television stations from Buffalo there was a meeting held of interested members who wanted to protest the possibility of such a thing happening. Five cabinet ministers showed up at that meeting, one of whom was the hon. member for Niagara Falls.
If the cabinet believes that the only right we should give to the public is that those licensed to carry out broadcasting undertakings must accept the responsibility to protect freedom of expression, why were those ministers protesting the move of the Barrie station? If the Barrie station had been moved it would have interfered only with our right to hear or receive programs from two Buffalo stations. We now have the minister stating that we are giving the broadcasters the right to freedom of expression, unquestionably. Why was there such a protest about the Barrie station moving into the Toronto area and interfering with the reception of two Buffalo stations? I still say that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.
If there were justification for protest against that threatened move by certain financial
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting interests, well known in this house, why have we taken the position of telling a C.A.T.V. operator that we are not interested in reception now but only interested in the unquestionable right of a station to broadcast? Only a few months ago five cabinet ministers were present at a meeting to protest this proposed move. As far as I can see now, two of those five at that meeting are here in the house. It is very strange that they were protesting about that interference with reception, but now tell us that all the government is willing to grant is the unquestionable right to freedom of expression. We are talking about the right to receive all programs that are available in an area. If the public wants to pay out money they should have the right to do so and get what they want in the area.
I can remember in the early days of radio, going back some 40 years now, when there was a big radio operation in Chicago which, over the course of the years, developed into one of the biggest radio houses in the world. That operation had the slogan "mighty monarch of the air", and hammered home again and again the advertising phrase "the air is full of things you should not miss". This phrase sold millions of radio sets in the United States and Canada. I am sure many members of this house will recall that advertising slogan. The operator of that station was not foolish enough to suggest that the air was full of things and we should not miss any of them. It is a simple fact that the public is only able to hear and understand one program at a time. This operation did not suggest that the air was full of things and we should not miss any.
We are not demanding that every program in an area should be made available to every Canadian who wants a C.A.T.V. installation. However, we are saying that if a Canadian family wants to pay money to get programs, other than those available to him through the local T.V. station, that family has the right to spend money to that end.
What justification is there for the statement that a C.A.T.V. application should be turned down because a second station may be built in an area? I am thinking of Napanee, Gana-noque, and Prescott, to which I referred some time ago by using a letter I received from the Secretary of State. We were told that the applications were turned down because the establishment of a second T.V. station in that general area might be inhibited. I pointed out at the time that the next station to go in there, according to the white paper and the
604S
January 26, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting report of the committee on broadcasting, would be a C.B.C. station. Certainly, any interference with a second station would not bother the C.B.C. because it pays no attention to money. Why should the people in the Prescott, Gananoque and Napanee area have been deprived of C.A.T.V. service in the past, at the present and for heaven knows how much longer, because the cabinet is rescheduling, prolonging and drawing out operations? We must bear in mind that the cabinet is cutting back the expenditures of all departments, including the C.B.C., in this rescheduling and drawing out operation. I say to you that as far as the residents of that area are concerned, the air is full of things they should not miss. Why do they have to wait until the cabinet finds there is enough money left over, after equalization payments to the provinces, to extend the C.B.C. into the Kingston area?
The people in these areas should have the opportunity of choice today. I could not agree less with that if there were 15 programs available in the Prescott-Napanee-Gananoque area. If they want a C.A.T.V. system with only five channels, that should be their choice.
There is one other point I should like to deal with in respect of what the Secretary of State said in commenting about the amendment of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. She talked about putting out signals. C.A.T.V. installations do not put out signals; they are only a reception area. They receive; they cannot put out signals under the licences that are granted to them by the Department of Transport. I am not arguing that C.A.T.V. should be given the right to put out signals; but when they are only receiving, why should there be a limit on the number of stations that can be licensed throughout the Dominion of Canada?
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I am old enough to remember the time when the government used to try and collect a little tax on radio receiving sets. I call it a tax, because if I am not mistaken it was $2 and at a later date it was increased to $2.50. A tax was put on receiving sets throughout Canada in the days of the Canadian Radio Commission, following the Aird report. If there ever was a more unpopular tax than even the tax on tea in Boston, it was that radio tax which the government tried to collect from the people of Canada. It was called, euphemistically, in government circles a


licence fee, but to the people who were called upon to pay it, it was a tax.
There are men in this house of an age to remember the days when an uproar developed with regard to this tax. If a family had two or three radios in its home, did they have to take out a licence in respect of each radio, or did the $2 licence fee cover the radios used by the household? The interpretation was first given that you had to have a $2 licence for each individual set. Then, there were radios in motor cars. The government had not changed its mind on the matter and said that you had to have a licence, or pay this fee, for a receiving set installed in a motor car.
I do not know whether this next statement is any credit to me or not. I think it is, although many in the house may disagree with me and think of it as a black mark against me. I can tell you that I am the man who said to Mackenzie King in the course of a general election, which the Liberals won, that they should remove that tax on multiple radio sets in homes and on radio sets in motor cars. If any hon. member wants to check on this he will find that there was a general election at that time and I made this suggestion. I came down from Toronto and the matter was discussed by a large number of Liberals.
Today we do not have a tax on receiving sets anywhere, and I do not think Canadians as a whole would go for it any more; they are much happier paying for the C.B.C. through the general taxation to which they are subjected than having people coming around and checking on the number of sets they have. Members of the house will remember that people used to go around counting the aerials over houses. Then people did not put aerials up, in order that the inspectors, as they were called, could not count them. The inspectors would then knock at the door and ask how many sets were in the house, because people were hiding the aerials. All that is past and gone, but not forgotten.
We have not imposed a licence fee or tax on receiving sets in years. Are we going back to that system now? I say to you, as a Liberal, that the public have the right to know. It is only about six years ago that the daily newspapers of Canada carried a tremendous advertising campaign, and the theme of it was the public's right to know. Is the cabinet of Canada, in 1968, going to deny the public's right to know by stating, "We will not put the C.A.T.V. system into this area in which somebody wants to operate a station, because the
January 26, 1968

local television operator might lose a little money if we did"? I could not care less whether the local television operator loses money as a result. Does the cabinet care about how much revenue the newspapers are losing to television? Why do they worry at this time about the local T.V. operator and whether or not he is losing money?
I would ask members of the house to read pages 166 and 167 of the report to which I have referred. This afternoon the hon. member for Queens was talking about the way in which C.B.C. puts programs over the air. He pointed out that when the C.B.C. starts to build up a program to prove that the earth is flat, they get the finest looking and most suave people they can find to prove that it is flat. Then, they get a bunch of dumb bunnies to prove that it is round. A few snide questions are asked about those who contend the world is round, thoughts are expressed on the other side, and finally the people appearing on the C.B.C. who contend the world is round are called "squares".
If you want to read some insinuating questions on this subject, read pages 166 and 167 of the committee report for November 6. You will find a T.V. station owner who is on the broadcasting committee of the House of Commons asking the very kind of question to which the hon. member for Queens referred today when he talked about a program to prove that the world is flat. The general tenor of the questioning on pages 166 and 167 is that C.A.T.V. systems will put the local stations off the air. I do not like to say it, but it is a straight statement of fact. He was questioning the Secretary of State, and she does not know too much about C.A.T.V.
In several places on those two pages she says that the local Canadian station is blanked out. I can only say that there is not a case in Canada where the local Canadian station is blanked out, but that answer is in this official government report. These are the answers of a lady who I think is smart, smart, smart. I have read those statements. The hon. Secretary of State said that she was not very familiar with the economics of this matter, and of her own knowledge she did not know much detail about it. We have her answers and are supposed to take them as being official. There are more facts on this subject than appear in the reports of the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts.
I do not think for one moment that the Secretary of State alone is responsible for the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting attitude that she is defending in the house. She said this afternoon, "I have to accept the opinion of the Department of Transport; I have to accept the opinion of the Board of Broadcast Governors". She would not be here piloting this bill through the house if she were not representing the idea of the entire cabinet as to suitable and satisfactory legislation with respect to a broadcasting policy for Canada.
I am certain that the cabinet does not know as much about C.A.T.V. as the Secretary of State. She has at least made a little study of it. I know a former member of the cabinet who knew a lot about C.A.T.V., because he was concerned with keeping it out of areas in which there were T.V. stations. He only kept it out because he knew a great deal about it. He was not interested in the welfare of the general public who were being deprived of programs because of his action.
I have said before that I have been hoping the cabinet would have the good sense to alter clause 2 (c), as suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. Perhaps the cabinet would propose a new clause or even withdraw the clause for a while until a clause could be inserted guaranteeing freedom of information to all and the right to receive information to all. But no, the Secretary of State stands up today and says she cannot accept the suggestion and justice department tells her she should not. She says, also, that the Board of Broadcast Governors advises her-you have to admit, informally-that she should not change the policy as expressed in clause 2 (c).
I have said before, and repeat again, that if this clause is passed by the Pearson administration, it will deny Liberalism. It will deny the public the right to know. I do not care how many people do or do not look at C.A.T.V. programs, but if there is somebody in Canada who wants to look at a C.A.T.V. program and there is a commercial operator ready to make the installation so that he can look at it, then the operator should be allowed to make the installation and the member of the public should be allowed to look at the C.A.T.V. programming. It is as simple as that.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I have protested against this ridiculous situation where the broadcaster has the right to express himself but the public does not have the right to receive these expressions if
6048	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting they so wish. I have mentioned before, possibly at a meeting of the committee on broadcasting, that some years ago I secured in Toronto the opinion of the supreme court of British Columbia regarding cablevision out there. In the committee I reminded the Secretary of State, who is an able lawyer, she had said to me in a private discussion one day that I should read the decision of the supreme court of British Columbia on the matter of cablevision because I would find the Canadian government had the right to tax and to licence the operators. I said to her in committee that I had obtained the decision of the supreme court of British Columbia and that I had had it for some years in Toronto. However, now that I was in Ottawa I would obtain another copy.
I received from the supreme court library xeroxed copies of the decision of the supreme court of British Columbia. The point at issue in this decision was that the province of British Columbia was endeavouring to regulate the C.A.T.V. receiving sets and to tax them on their commercial business. The cablevision operators objected to coming under provincial control. They went to the court on the matter, and the province of British Columbia, through the public utilities commission, prosecuted the Victoria Cablevision Limited and two other receiving station operators. The decision was that cablevision does not come within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments but is a federal matter. It is interesting to note the various references made by the judges of the British Columbia supreme court by previous decisions of the Privy Council that the transmitting of a signal and its reception cannot be separated.
The province of British Columbia was trying to do that very thing by arguing that the C.A.T.V. installation in British Columbia, which was receiving signals from, say, the United States came under provincial jurisdiction and therefore the province could tax and regulate it. The judges of the supreme court of British Columbia dismissed the argument of the province and said it was a federal matter. I would draw the hon. members' attention to the fact that the decision of the supreme court of British Columbia handed down on March 22, 1965, has never been appealed.

I think this has not been the case during recent years in the programming by the C.B.C. and by private television, although I believe we are dealing strictly with the public broadcasting corporation.
What concerns me about the general trend of programming is the responsibility which the public broadcasting corporation bears in this respect, and with which we cannot deal

effectively in the house, toward those institutions in our country that form the very fibre, the very warp and woof, of the Canadian way of life. I am concerned, too, about those younger people who do not have the selective ability to turn off the television set when there is something on it which they do not wish to see or which perhaps they should not see.
