speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved
maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-19, an act respecting the right of privacy.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to Bill No. C-19, an act respecting the right of privacy, since the subject is of great importance to the maintenance of democratic institutions and procedures. It is of increasing importance in the type of society that is evolving today.
Right of Privacy Act of 1967
I first heard of wire tapping just before the first world war when the miners of Sandon and Silverton in the Slocan country were on strike. The miners discovered that management was wire tapping conversations between the two villages of Sandon and Silverton. After the miners discovered this, they got two Gaelic speaking miners to carry on all discussions over the telephone, and from that time on management was in a bit of a fog.
I next heard of wire tapping when wire tapping was used with respect to certain illegal information in connection with race track results and things like that. The information relayed related to gamblers who were carrying on their work illegally. Then, throughout the years, I heard of wire tapping again in connection with its use, along with certain other mechanical devices, by spying agencies and those who were engaged in criminal activities.
Since then I have read numerous books, such as "The Intruders"-The invasion of privacy by government and industry-by Senator Edward B. Long, and "The Eavesdroppers" by Samuel Dash.
This matter came to prominence generally to the people of Canada when a landed immigrant, E. P. O'Neal, otherwise known as "Casey" bugged the meetings of the pulp and paper workers of Canada in Vancouver as the result of co-operation with personnel of the R.C.M.P. At that time, Lloyd Craig, who was a personal friend of mine and well known to me, died in his bedroom. I might say that his loss is mourned by the entire community of Castlegar and by all those in the trade union movement who respected his character, his integrity and what he tried to do for the formation of the Canada pulp and paper workers union organization in British Columbia.
May I quote from the report of the commission of inquiry into invasion of privacy. I wish to quote part of that report to indicate the urgent need for amendment to the Criminal Code to correct the situation. I shall begin quoting part of the report at page 4:
The chief officers of the International Union became alarmed at what was happening and contacted a man who was going under the name of E. P. O'Neal at that time and who was then secretary of the British Columbia Federation of Labour and employed him as an organizer to attempt to bring order out of the chaos which had arisen.
The report then goes on to say:
The pulp and paper workers of Canada organization scheduled a convention at the Ritz Hotel in Vancouver for November 5, 1966. O'Neal conceived
January 26, 1968

Right of Privacy Act of 1967
the idea of attempting to ascertain knowledge of their future actions and plans. He already was acquainted with two officers of the security and intelligence branch of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and discussed his problem with them.
I shall deal at greater length with the activities of these gentlemen on this subject at a more appropriate time. I continue:
As these two individuals, Cpl. Reed and Const. Ouellette were in that branch of the force to which the questions of security of the state are assigned they were naturally interested as policemen in some of the individuals who were taking part in the activities of this union. There is no evidence as to the background of these individuals but I have no doubt that their reputations and actions were discussed.
It is clear that the three of them discussed the best ways and means of obtaining the information that O'Neal sought. The corporal suggested to O'Neal that he might plant an informer in their group and procure some information. With this advice O'Neal did not agree. There were several discussions during which O'Neal raised the question as to the use of "bugging" devices and asked them if they could recommend someone who could render him such a service.
The officers at first decided against taking this step but subsequently they called a private detective named Bud Graham who had been a former member of the force and who had served along with Reed and told him that he would be called by a "labour leader or someone high up in the movement." Then Reed advised O'Neal to contact Graham and make his own arrangements with regard to the undertaking he wished him to take on.
At this juncture it may be appropriate to consider the position of the force as a whole. Counsel for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police asked that I find that as a force that body was in no way involved in the events which took place in the first week of November at the hotel. Counsel further asked me for a finding to that effect.
In considering this request I am faced with the fact that no evidence was tendered by the force as such, although a responsible officer of that body was at Miss Christie's elbow instructing her at all times. Any cross-examination which might have elicited the facts was strenuously objected to, and finally ended in the filing of an affidavit of the minister claiming privilege and the invoking of the Official Secrets Act. All of these actions effectively stopped any evidence being elicited which would have enabled me to decide whether or not Reed and Ouellette were conducting a "caper of their own."
Reed and Ouellette are experienced members of the force. At the time of their interviews with O'Neal and with Graham and all their subsequent actions they were officers in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police as a force has not taken any steps to explain its position and I find it impossible, unless there is evidence to the contrary, to come to the conclusion under the circumstances that any information obtained by officers of the law was not obtained officially. Consequently, I feel I cannot come to the conclusion that the force has divorced itself from the actions of Reed and Ouellette.

My one criticism of those two officers is they did not clearly impress Bud Graham with the fact that his employment by O'Neal was in no way official and that O'Neal was employing him to further his own ends. They certainly left the impression but not the word wTith Bud Graham that employment by O'Neal was official. Mr. Graham, stated that he had a clear impression that what he was doing was for the general benefit of Canada and helping the force of which he had formerly been a member, which statement I accept.
Graham, after consultation with O'Neal, arranged for quarters in the Ritz Hotel and proceeded to plant his devices. From these he was able to monitor or tape all conversations that took place not only in the convention but also in the bedrooms of the leaders of this movement.
One room that was monitored was the bedroom of Lloyd Craig who at that time was president of the Pulp and Paper Workers of Canada. His room was shared with one, Macphee, who apparently was the "Grey Eminence" of the movement. Craig was suffering from a grave deterioration of his internal organs including his heart. During the night before the convention opened he died.
I wish to refer to one or two other statements in this report.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I find that as the law now stands Graham is in no way to be censured for his actions. What he did was done on the advice of his counsel. O'Neal himself was advised by Graham that he, O'Neal, had nothing to fear from the police as no crime had been committed and advised him not to admit anything. O'Neal did not take legal advice and instead of evading questions or stating "no comment" gave a blanket denial to the newspapers in which he denied any knowledge of the facts narrated by Graham. This denial Mr. Fleishman submitted triggered him in his subsequent actions and advice, which have already been characterized above.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, when Mr. O'Neal was giving evidence under oath before the judge he had to admit that he had told a confounded lie on that occasion. I mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that there is nothing in the law to prevent this type of operation being conducted in the country at this time. That is why I, among others in this party and I am sure in the house as well, am keen to get the situation remedied.
I should like to quote an article from the Toronto Star for August 31, 1966, which indicates what can be done in this respect:
Ben Jamil, head of Continental Telephone Supply Co. in New York city, which claims to be the biggest manufacturer of electronic bugs, told the Star he has made whopping sales to the Canadian government.
Mr. Jamil, inventor of the olive-in-a-martini transmitter (the toothpick is the antenna), says $30 million worth of bugs were sold to Canada by his and associated TJ.S. companies "in less than a year-the past year."
January 26, 1968

Though the majority of the equipment went to private and industrial buyers, "a healthy proportion was sold to the Canadian government," Jamil said.
Was much of this destined for the R.C.M.P. directorate?
"It wouldn't be fair for me to tell," Jamil replied. "Why don't you ask them?"
By "them" he means the Canadian government.
I should also like to read a brief extract from "Current History" for July, 1967:
Wiretapping and electronic eavesdropping: Con
The right to privacy is indeed the most comprehensive of all rights. A society which cherishes liberty and human dignity cannot do without it; a society which seeks to suppress freedom cannot tolerate it.
Then the Toronto Star for September 7, 1967 carried the heading "Lawyers asked to demand ban on bugging except by police". According to the article, at a meeting in Quebec city lawyers were asked to pass a resolution that was drafted by the Civil Liberties and Criminal Justice sections of the Canadian Bar Association for submission to a convention. I understand that that resolution was later adopted almost unanimously with provisions to protect our national security and to deal with certain very difficult criminal elements.
I should also like to quote briefly from the Ottawa Journal for August 25, 1967. I was very pleased to read this statement. The report is datelined Calgary and reads as follows:
Solicitor General Pennell said Wednesday electronic eavesdropping and wiretapping should be banned except for national security purposes and crime fighting, with permission given by a court.
I hope the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) will remind the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) that he has failed to include an amendment of this type in his bill which makes many worthy amendments to the Criminal Code. I am pleased to hear that the Solicitor General is in favour of legislation to stop invasion of privacy by wire tapping and other mechanical methods of eavesdropping, but I repeat that I hope he brings this question to the attention of the Minister of Justice before the bill amending the Criminal Code is finally adopted so that a clause dealing with this very important subject can be included.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that all bills on the order paper concerned with this subject should be referred to the justice and legal affairs committee of the House of Commons for consideration along with the present
Right of Privacy Act of 1967 amendments proposed to the Criminal Code. This would give an opportunity to hear witnesses on the matter and to make a report to parliament.
My bill, Mr. Speaker, simply undertakes to deal with this situation. It provides for the protection of our national security and makes provision for dealing with certain criminal elements.
Clause 6 of my bill reads as follows:
Sections 3 and 4 of this act shall not apply where a person is duly authorized in writing by a judge of a Superior Court of criminal jurisdiction to conduct a search or investigation, at the request of the Minister of Justice of Canada, in cases affecting the national security of Canada.
Clause 7 provides:
Sections 3 and 4 of this act shall not apply in the case of a peace officer or other person acting in the course of his duties and duly authorized in writing by a Justice of the Peace or a Magistrate to conduct a search or investigation for the purpose of the administration of justice, at the request of the Attorney General of the province concerned.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, paraphrasing the explanatory notes of the bill, may I point out that Mr. Justice Brandeis has referred to the right of privacy as being the right most valued by civilized men. Several outstanding jurists in Canada share the same opinion, and I am glad that the Solicitor General also shares that opinion. It is advisable to protect that right adequately and to stop the various forms of invasion of privacy.
The purpose of this bill is to provide that wire tapping and eavesdropping are prohibited except in the case of the administration of justice and the security of the state. I know other hon. members want to say a few words on this bill, so I shall be very pleased to resume my seat at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Mafheson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), particularly on an occasion such as this when he has given such thoughtful consideration to a matter which affects fundamental civil liberties.
It has been said that it was relatively simple to prohibit snooping by eavesdropping in the days when the human ear was the sole instrument for picking up sound; but today there are so many sophisticated electronic devices which do the same job without the snooper being anywhere near the premises that a whole new range of considerations apply.
The kind of equipment reported used by the Sargent inquiry will soon be considered
6052	COMMONS
Right of Privacy Act of 1967 primitive in comparison with gadgets that we are now told are being tested. I understand that it is possible to direct electronic beams from far away on to a window pane to pick up its vibrations and translate them into sounds, thus eavesdropping on conversations in the room behind the window.
George Orwell forecast that by 1984 dictators or governments will be able to listen in on everything that is going on behind closed doors. It will soon be possible to bug every cottage and boardroom in the country.
The question then arises what do we do about this? My hon. friend from Kootenay West has presented a constructive and responsible bill which certainly requires the most serious consideration. I suppose the most recent event to cause widespread interest was that arising from the royal commission of Judge R. A. Sargent. According to the Vancouver Sun for August 10, 1967 the royal commission conducted by Judge Sargent on the invasion of privacy heard more than 100000 words of evidence from 80 witnesses during 57 days of public hearings between December and June of last year.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The inquiry was triggered by the electronic bugging of a Pulp and Paper Workers of Canada union convention last November.
The Daily Colonist of Friday, October 18, last says:
Snooping of this modem kind is abhorrent in principle, and creates mechanical Peeping Toms to an extent that could be dangerous ... It strikes at the root of individual freedoms.
The Victoria Daily Times has this to say:
It is an integral part of the free and democratic system of life in Canada that the state shall not infringe on personal rights, and privacy is a right which will have to be more jealously guarded as time goes on-
Commissioner Sargent would make unauthorized eavesdropping a crime, along with possession of equipment which is capable of infringing privacy or receiving or monitoring police calls-
The inquiry conducted by Judge Sargent has stimulated serious consideration particularly on the west coast, by members of the Canadian Bar Association, civil liberty groups and by concerned citizens. The Montreal Star of August 18 says:
Electronic eavesdropping-whether it be wire tapping or some other form of bugging-is a repugnant invasion of the right to privacy. And the bugging business is booming. It has become a tool of industrial espionage, it has been employed by labour unions in jurisdictional disputes, it has been used by individuals to eavesdrop on their neighbours and their spouses.
[Mr. Matheson.l
DEBATES	January 26, 1968
But to suggest an absolute prohibition against the practice might, in special circumstances, endanger the national security.
This is along the lines of the remarks made by my distinguished and experienced hon. friend. The article continues:
There is merit in some of the recommendations of the British Columbia's one-man Royal Commission into the Invasion of Privacy by R. A. Sargent, a retired county court judge. He has called for legislation outlawing electronic eavesdropping by anyone except police and federal authorities under restricted conditions, and he has suggested that the mere possession of equipment capable of infringing privacy or receiving or monitoring police calls be made a crime.
The editorial concludes:
The safeguarding of individual liberty must be a primary aim of any democratic society. The Prime Minister has called for a conference of federal and provincial governments to establish a bill of rights for all Canadians; we recommend that the right to privacy be included.
I know that the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) who is an experienced advocate and a person to whom much of the responsibility in this field has been assigned is, along with his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), deeply concerned about this problem. The Sun of Saturday, August 19, makes a contribution which is worth bearing in mind. It says, quoting the fourth amendment to the United States constitution:
The right of the people to be secure In their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue but upon probably cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.
The editorial concludes with the words of Judge Louis D. Brandeis of the United States supreme court:
The most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized man is the right to be left alone.
On this, the writer comments:
The IT.S. Supreme Court knocked out blanket warrants because they provide no adequate judicial supervision or protective procedures. It acknowledged the seriousness of the crime situation in that country but asserted it was not right that the freedom of the many should be sacrificed to combat a relatively few members of society who do wrong.
What can be done about this situation? The question has been raised whether it affects, primarily, property and civil rights and ought therefore to come within provincial jurisdiction or whether in fact it is an area which can be dealt with under the Criminal Code. It has been suggested in British Columbia that there
January 26, 1968

should be safeguards introduced and penalties imposed to discourage the use or possession of electronic listening devices.
The attorney-general of that province, Mr. Bonner, feels that the appropriate statute is the Criminal Code of Canada under federal jurisdiction which would ensure uniform enforcement of "anti-bugging" laws in all the provinces.
A few days ago I was reading the biography of Norman Birkett "The Life of Lord Birkett of Ulverston" by H. Montgomery Hyde. Many of us recall that this great jurist was in Ottawa in 1947 and that he spoke with great effect in Washington before the bar association in 1950. I note, according to this biography, that in 1957, he was asked by the British prime minister, Mr. Macmillan, to become chairman of a small committee of Privy Councillors which all three political parties in parliament had agreed should hold an immediate inquiry into the exercise of the prerogative power of the Home Secretary of intercepting telephone communications-telephone tapping as it was commonly known. Lord Birkett, as he later became, was of Liberal persuasion. The other members of the committee were Lord Monckton representing the Conservatives and Mr. Patrick Gordon Walker for the Labour party.
The committee was given the widest possible terms of reference, in particular to consider and report upon under whose authority, to what extent and for what purposes this power had been exercised and to what use information so obtained had been put, and to recommend whether, how, and subject to what safeguards this power should be exercised and in what circumstances information obtained by such means should properly be used or disclosed. Incidentally, I believe that at this stage none of us who are now speaking to this bill know what actual conditions and practices prevail in Canada. I, certainly, do not have this information; I am not aware of any of the facts.
The report which Birkett himself drafted was presented to parliament, and contained these interesting conclusions;
1.	The right of the power to Intercept communications can only be surmised, but the power has been exercised from very early times; and has been recognized by a succession of statutes covering the last 200 years or more.
2.	The power is identical with the power to open letters and rests on the ancient power to intercept communications.
I might mention that there is another view, namely that the power rests on a compara-
Right of Privacy Act of 1967 tively modern statute, the Telegraph Act of 1868.
3.	The power to intercept communications is exercised for the prevention and detection of serious crime and for the preservation of the safety of the State.
4.	The power is now almost exclusively exercised by the Metropolitan Police, the Board of Customs and Excise and the Security Service. It is used with the greatest care and circumspection, under the strictest rules and safeguards, and never without the personal considered approval of the Home Secretary.
5.	The use of the power has been effective in detecting major criminals and preventing injury to national security.
6.	The exercise of the power in these limited spheres should be allowed to continue under the same strict rules and supervision and in the special circumstances set out above.
e (5:30 p.m.)
And finally:
7. The interference with the privacy of the ordinary law-abiding citizen or with his individual liberty is infinitesimal and only arises as the inevitable result of intercepting the communications of some wrongdoer. It has produced no harmful consequences.
My hon. friends who are interested may read the report of the committee of privy councillors appointed to inquire into the interception of communications which was presented to the British parliament in October, 1957, and may note that Mr. P. Gordon Walker, the labour member, had minor reservations which are contained on page 38 of the committee's report. Some of these are rather interesting, and are worthy of being referred to right now. I shall do so only in summary form. Mr. Gordon Walker stated:
In my opinion public concern about telephone tapping is such that if the interception of communications for the detection of crime continues as in the past there may be some danger of a weakening of the popular approval without which the police cannot in the long run carry on effectively.
I think that is a novel, ingenious, and probably very wise argument. He also said:
One of the factors determining the evolution of policy in regard to the interception of communications has been the state of public opinion towards the exercise of this power. .. the interception of letters to prevent the transmission of illegal lottery material was abandoned in November 1953; shortly afterwards the interception of letters believed to contain obscene matter was similarly discontinued. In my view the interception of communications should never have been used for either of these purposes;-
Mr. Gordon Walker concluded:
Public repugnance to the interception of communications has, it seems to me, increased and there should therefore be a further restriction
6054	COMMONS
Right of Privacy Act of 1967 upon the use of this power for the purposes of the detection of crime. In future the interception of communications should, in my submission, no longer be regarded as an admissible method of detection in what may be called ordinary cases of crime ... but should be authorized only when the Secretary of State is satisfied that there is the most extreme and urgent reason.
He goes on to spell out what he means.
The application of these new and much stricter standards of judgment by the Secretary of State should, I suggest, be such that the interception of communications for the detection of crime would in practice cease to be used for long periods of time. It would be a power held in reserve for unusual and extraordinary cases of the utmost urgency, in which there could be no doubt that the use of the power would carry overwhelming public support.
He makes a distinction between interception of communications for the detection of crime and for security reasons and purposes, and I think this is borne out by every study of the matter made throughout the world. Mr. Gordon Walker made this important point:
A far larger proportion of the information that the security service must discover is obtained by interception of communication than in the case of the Police or the Customs. A great deal of this vital information could be discovered by no other means. There cannot, therefore, in my view be the same sharp restriction of the use of the interception of communications by the Security Service as I recommend in regard to the use of this power for the detection of crime.
Even in the field of security the strictest possible limits should be set to the use of the power to intercept communications.
Then he states out what he thinks are two legitimate considerations, as follows:
(1)	direct counter-espionage and protection of high secrets of State;
I doubt that there is anybody who would seriously challenge that conclusion. Then he sets out the second, and remember that this is Mr. P. Gordon Walker of the Labour party:
(2)	the prevention of the employment of Fascists or Communists in connection with work, the nature of which is vital to the state.
Anyone who has gone into the recent studies resulting from the defection some years ago of Philby, and noted the inter-relationships between the various departments of the British government as they may relate to defence and foreign affairs, must appreciate that here we are dealing with an extremely sensitive area.
It is interesting to look at page 41 of the report of the committee of privy councillors inquiring into the interception of communications in Brtiain. On that page there is a table listing the number of interceptions authorized

DEBATES	January 26, 1968
by the British secretary of state. Running through the years from 1937 to 1956 I notice that under the heading "Police, Customs, Post Office and Security," interceptions by telephone totalled as few as 17 in any one year and never went higher than 231, and I would point out that this is in the United Kingdom which has a population several times that of Canada. The figure for the interception of letters is somewhat larger, ranging from a low of 90 in 1945 up to 1,192 in 1940.
Under the heading "Drugs, Lotteries and Obscene Publications" only ten interceptions by telephone are recorded, all of these taking place in the year 1955. Interception by letters ranged in total from as few as two in some years to a high of 714, and in five of the years from 1937 to 1956 there were no letter interceptions whatever. I believe these figures show the great reserve in the use of this power in Britain. They demonstrate that this privilege of the British secretary of state has been used with great circumspection, and I believe there has been no serious challenge to the conclusions of this committee which indicate that this power has been used wisely and well.
I congratulate the hon. member on his contribution to a very important subject. I have no doubt that there is much classified information available to the government. If not there will be shortly, when the royal commission on security reports, which will assist parliament to do the right and wise thing to preserve the high standard that now prevails in this country and, if anything, see to it that that standard is enhanced and improved.

maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the story of wire tapping, eavesdropping and bugging is in a sense the story of the erosion of our own personal rights and freedoms as science enables us to extend our ears to listen in many directions, even through walls and into places we cannot get physically. At the outset of my remarks, I wish to correct one false impression which the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) may have left with the house when he said that in the case in British Columbia Craig died from a bug. I want to correct that. Craig died from heart failure; he did not die of a bug.

maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I read it into the record that he had this heart trouble. I did not suggest he died from a bug.

maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad that we now have that corrected. Eavesdropping is an
January 26. 1968

antique word, describing the act of hanging around the outside of a house or window to hear what is going on inside. Science has enabled us to progress ever since we began to learn something about electrical communication.
Wire tapping is also a pretty old word which is still in use. It describes the act of tapping into a wire and physically attaching something to it whereby one can listen to a conversation being conducted over the wire. More recently there came the word "bugging", but even it is fairly old. It refers to devices which pick up signals from an induction current wire, and which magnify the sound coming from a considerable distance away, thus enabling people to listen through walls and across considerable distances. More modern devices are coming into use all the time, and they are being used by all sorts of people to pry into other people's affairs.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
These devices are not used just by criminals. As was pointed out by the commission of inquiry which investigated the invasion of privacy in British Columbia, automobile dealers in the city of Vancouver have found listening devices to be very handy in determining what price to set on a car. You simply walk into the car lot where you are met by a man known in the trade as a "liner". His job is to show you up and down the line of cars until you get an idea of the kind of car you want to buy. When you are hanging around a certain car looking as if you are about to talk seriously about it, he brings in a man known as a "closer". This is a man who is able to close a contract. He has the confidence of management. This man takes you into a little room where he discusses the price with you while the manager listens over the bugging device. Then he excuses himself from the room. I do not know for what reason, but we all know that we have to excuse ourselves from time to time.
After the "closer" leaves the room, the man and his wife talk together while he and the manager listen to the conversation. They speak about the price of the car. The woman tells the husband the amount of money he is able to spend. So, the manager and the "closer" then discuss what the price should be, what the offer will be, and then return to the room where the deal is closed. It works very well. The best automobile companies in Vancouver were using this method. These people appeared on the stand and gave evidence before the commission of inquiry into the
Right of Privacy Act of 1967 invasion of privacy. For weeks after that, one could hardly get anybody in Vancouver to buy a car except in the middle of a field. This is an example of commercial bugging used every day in business.
Some of the other ways in which bugging can be carried on are interesting. I should like to cite a few of these in case hon. members should run across them in the course of their duties in the House of Commons or when they go to cocktail parties. I should like to quote from the Ottawa Citizen story by Bruce Phillips of February 20, 1965. This story comes from Washington. The article begins by asking a question:
Are you a martini drinker? Be careful the next time you take one. It may be listening to you.
It sounds outlandish and it is, but the electronic martini (microphone in the olive, antenna in the toothpick), is only one of a bizarre collection of snooping devices paraded before a senate investigating committee this week.
Then in a later paragraph the article continues:
As a dramatic demonstration, the committee chairman, Senator Edward V. Long, was startled to be told by one of the witnesses that a bowl of roses on his desk was bugged.
There are paragraphs which contain some explanation of some of the other devices currently in use:
A small dish-type antenna, freely available through the mail-order catalogues, called the "big ear", which magnifies sound a million times and can monitor conversations a block away. It costs $18.95.
That would be plus the tariff, exchange and sales tax if one were to buy it in Canada.
A laser-type beam which can be aimed at a room several blocks away and transmit back a television picture, with sound.
A small transmitter which can monitor telephone conversations from any distance, and is practically undetectable.
Then, the writer gives some advice concerning what we should do in this kind of world:
People who must talk in a room, he said, should unplug the telephone, turn on the shower and bathroom faucets, and turn on a radio or television set full volume.
We need to do that in caucus, but we do not have any taps there to turn on.
A private detective from San Francisco, Harold Lipset, showed some of the devices perfected on the west coast. They include a tie-clip microphone, an ordinary office stapler concealing a microphone, and a portrait with a transmitter buried in the framing.
6056	COMMONS
Right of Privacy Act of 1967
Mr. Lipset said there were 10,000 businesses in northern California alone which used devices to spy on their employees, and without citing his source he said 5,000 federal government offices also have snooping equipment.
In such a world what can we do to defend ourselves? I have here a number of clippings dealing with the ways in which such devices are used in Canada. This is not simply information which came from United States stories concerning uses there. This has to do with usage on this side of the border. The library of the House of Commons keeps a considerable file known under the old fashioned phrase "wire tapping". In that file one finds all sorts of clippings dealing with the amount of bugging which goes on in Canada. The following appears in the Ottawa Citizen for April 9, 1964:
Ernest Nuttall, 63, whose testimony helped acquit John Wasylenchuk of Burnaby, B.C., of second-degree murder charges in Seattle last week, said his own telephone was tapped.
"People have no idea of the extent of wiretapping today," he said in an interview. "They would be amazed."
Nuttall said: Police secretly have telephone company officials make records of telephone conversations.
In the same story another policeman denies this. Then, there is a story in the Edmonton Journal for August 12, 1964 which in part reads as follows:
Thomas O'Dwyer, an Edmonton real estate man who has become a central figure in a mysterious controversy involving the Alberta government, said Tuesday he suspects his phone is being tapped by the RCMP.
In another dispatch of the Canadian Press from Toronto which appears in the Ottawa Journal for May 6,	1964 we find the
following:
A Conservative member of the legislature said Tuesday that wire tapping and "bugging" of private conversations is prevalent in his own community of London, and probably throughout Ontario.
John White (PC

London South) told Attorney-General Wishart that auto dealers in London and the Bell Telephone Company used concealed microphones to listen in on conversations.
Then in the Toronto Globe and Mail for August 28, 1964 we find the following:
A. W. Miller, a lawyer who has acted for several clients whose phones were tapped, will contend that the law, the only one of its kind in Canada, is ultra vires, and should be quashed.
This was in respect of a bylaw in the city of Edmonton which would prevent wire tapping.
There is plenty of evidence in these clippings concerning wire tapping of all kinds

DEBATES	January 26, 1968
which is done commercially, which is done criminally, which is done by the police and which is done every day in major cities across Canada. The argument made on the side of the authorities is that crime proliferates in our cities and that they in turn use these scientific devices so that they can pry into the bedrooms or bug our paper clips in order to prevent crime and combat it. This is a danger to freedom. It constantly erodes our freedom. We will not be able to live as we have lived in the past under the old laws which denied police officers the right to use bugging devices to combat crime. At the same time, the criminal will have all the advantages of using these devices for the purpose of committing crime.
When we consider passing legislation of this kind which empowers a person to use such devices, we must remember that we are slowly eroding away a piece of our own freedom and that we must do it only after careful thought.
9 (5:50	p.m.)
This is not really the only way in which we are eroding our freedoms today as a result of the science we are building around us. Here, in the government, we are adding more and more computers to our operations. As these computers become more sophisticated and are able to contain more information, as they are cross-linked and connected with each other, we are approaching the day when the government will be able to press a button and up will pop instant history. The computer will provide statistics regarding our health, our finances, our ability to pay our bills, our army records, the number of times we have passed through stop streets or violated parking meters and all sorts of things. This information will be placed on cards and stored as a record of our actions. Whatever we build by way of communication devices may extend our capability and may improve our standards of living, but at the same time will mean we must live more and more in glass houses. That is perhaps one of the penalties we pay for the kind of progress we are making in the whole field of communications.

maintopic: RIGHT OF PRIVACY ACT OF 1967 MEASURE TO PROVIDE SAFEGUARDS, PENALTIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) deserves our compliments for taking a different approach to the suggested legislation respecting the right of privacy. He seeks not to amend the Criminal Code but brings a new bill before us which highlights the right of privacy, not the right to invade it.
January 26, 1968

I submit we should not develop a national anxiety neurosis about wire tapping and bugging devices. I know when the hon. member for Kootenay West travels westward to his home on the Kettle Valley railway he has time to worry that possibly these things are present around him. I should like to submit that all these measures of private members, of a similar vein, should not be pressed at the present time. Not only is the Department of Justice hard pressed with other Criminal Code amendments and the upcoming federal-provincial conference on the constitution, but there are other valid reasons for taking a little more time before bringing into force any legislation analogous to the legislation put forward by many members.
First of all, the report of the royal commission on security has not been tabled. It likely will take a very careful look at this whole field of wire tapping and will make recommendations. When the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), of a similar vein, was being debated, we learned that the Canadian Bar Association had this whole matter under consideration. Although the bar association did not get far with this subject at the last annual meeting, apparently it will be thoroughly studied in the interim. Likely when the next meeting is held in September of this year we will receive a very thorough and considered report on the views of that association. It seems to me there is not so much urgency about this matter that we would be prevented from waiting until we hear from this learned body.
I agree that this field needs to be controlled and regulated, but there is no necessity for ill-advised haste in this connection. I should hope that members will stand bills of this nature until next September rather than press forward with them. That is my own personal view of the matter. I am advised that the Department of Justice has received a number of recommendations in respect of wire tapping and electric eavesdropping devices. The deputy attorney general of British Columbia has forwarded a resolution of the Vancouver city council in favour of a Criminal Code amendment restraining wire tapping.
Business of the House
By a resolution dated October 26, 1964, the council of the corporation of the city of Toronto indicated that it is categorically opposed to the unrestricted use, whether in the process of law enforcement or otherwise, of any kind of mechanical or electronic device for intercepting or overhearing words spoken in conversation by one person to another, not intended to be heard by the person using such device. They expressed the belief that the use of such device is an offence against an individual's right to privacy, and as such should be forbidden under all circumstances except where a superior court judge otherwise orders for the purpose of criminal investigation.
The bill at hand, of course, recommends that a peace officer or magistrate have the power to otherwise order the use of these devices. The Bell Telephone Company of Canada, by a letter dated February 14, 1966, urged in fact that the government sponsor legislation in respect of wire taping and offered in co-operation in studying the subject.
